Rules that follow:

- **No pill is the all-clear, and it is never given before a check.** The pill is drawn only while OrcaSlicer reports an issue, ignored ones included. While OrcaSlicer holds an unapplied edit the last issues are kept, the pill says it is checking and both buttons are off, so the pill does not go until OrcaSlicer has looked. An issue that was not in the list before is announced once by a ring that spreads from the pill twice; an edit that keeps an issue, and ignoring one or undoing that, announce nothing.
- **Nothing is resolved by the fork.** An issue goes when OrcaSlicer lets go of its notification. An agent saying it fixed something changes nothing.
- **"Blocks printing" is OrcaSlicer's answer.** An error-level notification blocks. For the slice result it is OrcaSlicer's own post-slice check, which allows a path 2 mm past the plate edge; the monitor does not apply a stricter test of its own.
- **The object is never read out of the words.** Two messages of one kind are told apart by comparing OrcaSlicer's words now with its words before, as OrcaSlicer does itself. Which object a message is about always comes from a check's own ids.
- **A press acts on what is true at the press**, and with no assistant set up it sends nothing and offers the chat panel's setup. **One button, one question**: Ask AI sends "Explain this issue and my options." with the issue as context, and the turn gets the ordinary tools, so the person asks for a fix in the chat. A second "Resolve with AI" button was removed on 2026-10-28: it sent the same context with the same tools and differed only in the sentence, which the person could not tell apart.
- **Slice-result warnings follow OrcaSlicer's send dialog.** The warnings the G-code processor stores on a slice result (bed temperature, nozzle hardness, timelapse) are shown as OrcaSlicer's Bambu send dialog shows them, the only place OrcaSlicer itself shows them: never the bed-temperature one, the traditional-timelapse one once although it is stored twice. The chip and `slice_report` read one fork-owned table, `Workspace/SliceResultWarnings`, whose comment says why it is a copy and not an upstream seam, and a guard test fails when OrcaSlicer defines a kind the table does not classify. The timelapse ones apply only to a print that records a timelapse, which is chosen when it is sent: `slice_report` and Check print list them marked so, and the chip does not count them.
- **Operation failures are not print issues.** A failed download or a refused arrange is a confirmation, never an entry in the issue list.
- **Closing hides, it never resolves.** The pill is always there and is the way back; the list and the bubble are opened and closed, one at a time, and closing either changes nothing about the issue or the count. The list closes on a pick, a second press of the pill, Escape, or a press outside it. The bubble belongs to the selection: opening it selects its object, and it closes when that object stops being selected, which is what a click on the empty plate, Escape and a click on another object already do in OrcaSlicer. Turning the view or dragging the object leaves it open. Its close button leaves the selection alone, and a press on **Ask AI** that reaches the chat closes it. With one issue the pill opens the bubble directly, and with several the bubble's pager walks them all. The overlay hears Escape and presses through handlers of its own on the canvas's window, bound after OrcaSlicer's and so called first; no OrcaSlicer file is involved.
- **Ignoring a warning is the person's mark, not OrcaSlicer's.** **Ignore this warning** in the bubble leaves OrcaSlicer's notification alone: the warning stays in the list, marked, below the ones that count, and the pill stops counting it ("1 warning ignored" when nothing else is left, never "No print issues"). Only a warning can be ignored; a blocker cannot, because OrcaSlicer would still refuse to print. An ignore lasts while OrcaSlicer keeps reporting that warning on the active plate's own list, and is forgotten when OrcaSlicer stops, so a warning that comes back is shown again. It is not saved with the project. The rule is `mark_ignored` in `PrintIssues/PrintIssue`.

Known limits: application and account notifications (update available, plug-in missing, preset sync conflict) are routed to `App` and drawn nowhere yet. A confirmation shows OrcaSlicer's words and a close button; the actions OrcaSlicer attached to its own notification (open folder, eject, cancel an upload) are not offered. Only a slice has a percentage and a known ending; other work shows a bar with no amount and is recorded as done unless its Cancel was pressed. Uploads and downloads have not been run. The tips and the object size card are not shown.

### Agent WebView

The production Agent interface is a separate React/TypeScript package that runs locally inside a `wxWebView`. It needs:

- a versioned schema for commands and events;
- scripted mock conversations that play back the same way every time, for UI tests;
127:Print again sends a recorded G-code's kept file, never a fresh slice, and always through OrcaSlicer's own send dialog, where the person presses Send. A Bambu printer takes a `.gcode.3mf`, so a Bambu print also keeps the package it uploaded (`<hash>.gcode.3mf`, and for a cloud printer the config 3MF it also sent), byte for byte, with its SHA-256 on the send (`packageHash`); it goes when its G-code's copy is pruned. Print again parses that package, hands it to Select Machine through `Plater::update_print_required_data` and `EVT_PRINT_FROM_SDCARD_VIEW` (the printer file browser's print-from-storage mode, which draws the plate, picture and filaments from the file), and sets the dialog's new-print flag (`SelectMachineDialog::set_required_data_new_print`, the one upstream seam), so the job uploads the local file as a new print instead of asking the printer to print by name. Printing from the printer's storage is not used: the file name on the printer is reused per project, so it cannot say which version would print. content.text:
The update check works. JusPrin 2.0.0 never pops up a prompt because it was designed that way: the result only ever appears in Preferences › Updates. I changed nothing.

**What the code does.** In [UpdateCheck.cpp](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Updates/UpdateCheck.cpp), the app checks GitHub 10 seconds after it starts, then again every hour. A check only runs if the last successful one was more than a day ago. When the check finds a newer version it saves it to the settings file and tells whoever is listening. Only one part of the app listens: the Preferences window ([PreferencesWindow.cpp:186](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Preferences/PreferencesWindow.cpp:186)). That window draws the dot beside "Updates" and the "JusPrin 2.0.1 is available" card. Home, the project screen, the gear icon and the chat never hear about it. Before JusPrin, OrcaSlicer had its own "new version" window that opened at startup. JusPrin turned that check off on purpose so OrcaSlicer's server is never asked ([ShellController.cpp:2094](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Shell/ShellController.cpp:2094)). So nothing else shows an update either.

**Where the design came from.** The JusPrin v2 design canvas has a note dated 2026-10-22 next to the Updates boards. It says the result shows "only here, plus the dot on Updates". It also says "Nothing pops up, and nothing appears in a project or in chat." The commit that added the check, 80ed1692ff on 2026-10-23, follows that note. I couldn't find your own words behind it: the session where it was decided isn't in the searchable transcripts. So it's unverified whether you chose "no pop-up" yourself or it was a proposal that got written down as decided.

**What this means for people already on 2.0.0.** Anything we change now only ships in a later release. People running 2.0.0 or 2.0.1 keep today's behaviour until they update by hand. Inside the app there's one other way to reach them. The server can refuse an old version, and the app then shows a "Get the new version…" button on the chat, sign-in and model picker. But that blocks their account, so it only makes sense when an old version really has to stop working. For the people on 2.0.0 now, the realistic routes are outside the app: an email, or a post where they already follow JusPrin.

**Decision needed: should JusPrin tell people about a new version anywhere besides Preferences?** It's your call because it changes what people see on screens outside Preferences, and the current design says nothing pops up.
- **Keep it as is.** Costs nothing. Most people will never find out a new version exists.
- **Put a dot on the gear icon on Home and on the project screen.** Small and quiet, about a day of work. It's still easy to miss, because the dot doesn't say what it means.
- **Show a one-line notice on Home once per new version.** For example: "JusPrin 2.0.1 is available", with Download and Skip buttons. It never appears inside a project or during a print. About a day or two of work plus new design boards. People can't miss it, and they can dismiss it.

My pick is the once-per-version notice on Home. If you agree, I'll draw the boards on the canvas first and build after you've seen them.
Yes, design a notice

The visual system (tokens, type, color, components, logo) lives in [Design system](design-system.md); this document does not repeat it. Design agents tend to write on-screen text that only they can read. The agent knows how the screen works, so a line like "The sixth digit signs you in." reads clearly to it and to any reviewer who knows the same. A person opening the app for the first time has to decode it, and often can't. The First-Launch Confusion Review (https://claude.ai/artifact/91wmdS3QU8UkzbPi1zog15, 2026-11-06) found 23 places on the first launch where a newcomer would misread or stall, and most of them were wording. The rules below exist to stop that at the source and to catch what still gets through. ## How a screen gets designed and checked These steps apply to every change to text a person sees, not only to new screens: a new link on an existing board, a reworded line, or a one-sentence fix all get the cold-reader check on the board before building (step 5) and in the running app after (step 8). 1. **Start from the person.** Before drawing, write down in two or three sentences who reaches this screen, what they know at that moment, what they came to do, and what they must decide here. Every line on the screen serves one of those. 2. **Draw the whole screen, not a component alone.** A board for review is the full screen at the app's size, with the header, panes and neighbouring content the person really sees there, on the JusPrin v2 canvas (https://claude.ai/artifact/ENCtdaz7gjynfbcy4JYbWJ). Build it from the Design System artifact's coded components and the app's own markup, never by copying an older board. Repeated compositions are imported by name, as [Design handoff requirements](design-system.md#design-handoff-requirements) rule 9 says. 3. **Fill it with real strings.** Text that summarises data comes from the rule that will produce it in the app, run on real data. If only a model could write a line, say so on the board. 4. **Write every line by the wording rule below.** 5. **Run the cold-reader check on the boards** (below). Rewrite and check again until every line and button reads as intended. 6. **Show the board for review by what a person sees.** Name the screen as the person would ("the welcome screen, after typing an email"), give the canvas page it is on, and attach the picture. Board ids and builder labels mean nothing to a reviewer. 7. **Build it** following [Writing UI code](design-system.md#writing-ui-code). 8. **Check it in the running app.** Take screenshots of the built screen along one real path and run the cold-reader check again. The guards prove the code went through the tokens; only the screenshots show what the person reads. ## The cold-reader check The writer of a screen cannot see that its text is cryptic, so the check is done by a reader who knows nothing about how the screen works. - Start a fresh agent. Give it only the screenshots and one or two sentences a real user would know (for example: "You own a 3D printer and just installed JusPrin, a desktop app that prepares 3D models for printing."). Give it no code, spec, design notes, chat history or list of suspected problems, and rename files so their names don't hint at anything. - Use screenshots from one coherent path, in the order a person meets them. Mixing signed-in and signed-out screens, or states set by hand, makes the reader report contradictions that no user would see. - Ask it, for each screen, to quote every line and every button exactly, say in one plain sentence what the line means or what the button will do, and list where it would hesitate, misread, worry, or not know what to do next, including information the screen leaves out. Tell it to read literally, like a busy newcomer: a line it had to puzzle out counts as a problem even if it worked it out. - Compare its answers with the intent written in step 1. Any line it reads differently from the intent gets rewritten, however small the gap. Its other hesitations are input to weigh, not orders. What the check is known to catch: on 2026-11-06 a fresh agent given only the review's ten screenshots fully caught 14 of the 23 problems and partly caught 4 more. It caught every cryptic phrasing in the list. It missed problems that need knowledge from outside the screen (that Skip installs a 250 mm Klipper printer) and finer editorial calls (a redundant reassurance, one allowance under three names, "Connected" used for an account). It also raised real questions the review had not, such as what happens after the free month. It has not been compared with a real first-time user, so for the screens that matter most, such as first launch, a person remains the final test. ## Wording Every line says what the person does or what happens to them, in a full sentence, in words a newcomer already has. The five patterns below are what the review found most. Each pair is the text the app showed and the review's proposed rewrite; the rewrites are proposals, not yet in the app. 1. **Facts joined by a middle dot.** The dot drops how the facts relate, and the reader guesses. - Before: "Signed in as new@example.com · 500 credits" (reads like a balance the person already had) - After: "You got 500 free credits for signing up.", with the email address on a smaller line under it 2. **Metaphors.** The reader has to work out what the image stands for. - Before: "New or existing account, same door." - After: a "Sign up free" button, with "Already have an account? Sign in" under it - Before: "Pick how the agent should think." (the options are ways to pay for or connect the agent) - After: "Sign up to use the AI agent, or skip it and just slice." 3. **Describing the mechanism instead of the action.** Say what the person does, not how the screen works inside. - Before: "The sixth digit signs you in. Read the email on any device." - After: "Type the code from the email. You can open it on your phone." 4. **Internal labels.** A name the team uses, shown nowhere else on the screen, explains nothing. - Before: "An Expert message is 5 credits." - After: the cost in things the person does, for example "500 credits is about 100 questions to the agent" (check the number against real costs) 5. **Hinting at a consequence instead of stating it.** If a choice changes what the person gets, say what it changes. - Before: "Skip, and JusPrin slices for a generic 0.4 mm printer until you add yours." - After: "If you skip, files are sliced for a stand-in printer with a 250 mm bed, not for yours. content.text:
I've drawn the notice. When a new version is out, a card appears at the top of Home's right column, above Printers. It's on the [JusPrin v2 canvas](https://claude.ai/artifact/ENCtdaz7gjynfbcy4JYbWJ#page-updating), page "Updating JusPrin", as boards 07 (light) and 08 (dark), and both are marked as a proposal. No code is written yet.

**What the card says** (the picture is attached above):
- **JusPrin 2.0.1 is available**
- "You have version 2.0.0. Your projects, printers and settings stay when you install the new one. Installing doesn't affect a print your printer is already running."
- **See what's new**: opens Preferences › Updates, which already shows the release notes.
- "The download page is on GitHub. Pick the file for your computer there: Mac, Windows or Linux."
- **Open download page ↗**: opens the GitHub release page, like Download in Preferences. The card stays until the new version is running.
- **Remind me tomorrow**: hides the card for 24 hours.
- **Skip this version**: works the same as Skip in Preferences. The card goes away, and it comes back when a newer release is out.

It never shows inside a project, in a chat or as a separate window. There's no card for a Microsoft Store install, or when automatic checks are off or stealth mode is on.

**What the wording checks changed.** Three fresh readers saw only the screenshot. The first draft quoted the opening line of the release notes. The reader didn't know "the printer chat" or what "languages that write decimals with a comma" meant, and those notes are in English only while the app now runs in 22 languages, so that line came out. Readers also hesitated in four other places:
- They expected "Download" to download a file, so it's now "Open download page".
- "Skip this version" was the only way to close the card and it sounded permanent, so I added "Remind me tomorrow".
- "Remind me later" didn't say when, which is why it now says tomorrow.
- One reader worried that installing would stop the print running on their printer, so the card now says it won't.

The third reader understood every line and all three buttons as intended. What they still wondered about (which file to pick, how to install) is answered on the GitHub release page itself.

**Still open:**
- The card promises that a running print keeps going while JusPrin is quit and reinstalled. I believe that's true for every connection type, because the printer runs the job on its own, but I haven't tested it. It should be checked before building.
- Anything built now only reaches people once they're on the release that contains it. People on 2.0.0 and 2.0.1 will never see this card, so reaching them needs an email or a post.

**Other canvas changes:**
- The Preferences note from 2026-10-22 that says "Nothing pops up" now has a line saying this proposal would replace that rule if you agree.
- No existing board needed marking as superseded, because the Home boards without the card still show Home when JusPrin is up to date.

# release. It never publishes anything.
#
# - The version is the one in src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Updates/Version.hpp, and
#   the draft is tagged jusprin/v<version>, as JusPrin 1.4.0 was (the repo
#   still holds OrcaSlicer's own v2.x tags). GitHub creates that tag only when
#   the draft is published, by hand, on the Releases page. JusPrin's update
#   check reads the public release list, which never includes drafts, so
#   users see nothing until then.
# - It stops if that version is already released, is not above every
#   released JusPrin version, or its tag already exists
#   (Packaging/release.mjs), and if

#   that the app shows under "What's new", is missing.

input.ask: Which update path should JusPrin take?

content.text:
It's moderately hard. With a full "Install and restart" button, I estimate two to three weeks of work, and most of the risk is on Windows. A smaller version, where the app downloads the installer and opens it for the person, would take a few days. Both figures are my estimates, not measurements.

**What JusPrin ships today**

- **Mac:** a signed and notarised disk image, so Apple accepts it as coming from us.
- **Windows:** an unsigned installer, plus a zip that runs without installing.
- **Linux:** an AppImage, a single file that runs as is.

OrcaSlicer has no in-app installer either, so there's nothing upstream to reuse.

**What "install and restart" takes on each platform**

- **Mac, about 3–5 days.** Sparkle is the standard tool for this. It downloads the update, checks it, swaps the app in place and relaunches. We would add Sparkle to the app bundle and keep a private signing key in the release workflow. Each release then signs its disk image and publishes a small list of versions for the app to read. The signing step needs care: Sparkle's helper programs must be signed one by one before the app itself ([Sparkle's publishing docs](https://sparkle-project.org/documentation/publishing/), [one developer's write-up of the pitfalls](https://steipete.me/posts/2025/code-signing-and-notarization-sparkle-and-tears)).
- **Windows, about 3–5 days, plus a decision for you.** WinSparkle, or our own code, would download the installer, check its signature, close JusPrin and run the installer silently. Our installer accepts the standard silent switch, `/S`. The catch is that our installer is unsigned. Having the app download and run an unsigned program on its own is the riskiest part of the whole plan, so the app must at least check a signature of our own on every download. Antivirus programs may also flag it. I haven't confirmed whether Windows' download warning (SmartScreen) fires for an installer the app downloads itself, so that has to be tested. Buying a Windows code-signing certificate removes most of this risk.
- **Linux, about 2–3 days.** AppImage has its own update mechanism, AppImageUpdate, which downloads only the parts of the file that changed ([AppImage docs](https://docs.appimage.org/packaging-guide/optional/updates.html)).

**What auto-update can't reach**

- People already on 2.0.0 and 2.0.1 must install the next version by hand once.
- The Windows zip and Microsoft Store installs can't update themselves. Store installs get updates from the Store anyway.
- A bug in the updater can strand people on that version, so each release needs a test of updating from the previous one.

**The smaller version.** PrusaSlicer does this in [its updater](https://github.com/prusa3d/PrusaSlicer/blob/master/src/slic3r/Utils/AppUpdater.cpp). It downloads the file inside the app. On Windows it runs the installer, and on Mac it opens the disk image in Finder for the person to drag across. On Linux it only downloads the file. That saves the trip to GitHub, but on Mac people still drag the app themselves. One person on Prusa's forum reported that the Mac update didn't replace the old app ([forum thread](https://forum.prusa3d.com/forum/prusaslicer/problems-with-automatic-update)).

**Decision needed: should JusPrin install updates itself, or only download them?**
- **Install and restart.** About two to three weeks, plus a Windows code-signing certificate if you want the Windows side safe and free of warnings. The card on Home would then offer "Install and restart" instead of "Open download page".
- **Download in the app only.** A few days. The person still runs the installer or drags the app, as today, just without visiting GitHub.
- **Keep the current card.** No extra work. People keep downloading from GitHub themselves.

My pick is Install and restart, built Mac first with Sparkle because that path is the most proven, and Windows only once the signing question is settled. Either way the card on Home is still needed, and only its buttons change.
